---
title: "How does k-means find groups nobody labelled?"
subtitle: "Guess some centres, give every point to its nearest one, move each centre to the middle of its points, and repeat until nothing changes."
engine: knitr
---

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="kmeans-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · all you are given: points, and no labels · made-up data"}
:::

SVM and KNN both started from **labelled** data. You knew which group each point belonged to, and the job was to learn the rule. Now take the labels away. You have a pile of customers, each with two measurements, and nobody has told you what kinds of customer there are. The question is whether natural groupings are hiding in the data.

This is **unsupervised learning**. There is no response variable and no right answer to check against, so the algorithm has to discover the structure on its own. [Exam trap: clustering has no response variable. "Find groups", "segment customers", "no labels" means clustering. "Classify", "predict the category", "labelled data" means classification (SVM, KNN). Do not confuse the two.]{.side}

## Assign, then move

k-means is a short loop. Pick $k$ random starting centres, called centroids. Assign each point to the nearest centre. Move each centre to the average of the points assigned to it. Repeat the last two steps until nothing changes. That is the whole algorithm.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="kmeans-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · one half-step per press: assign, move, assign, move · made-up data"}
:::

The figure opens just after the first assignment, with every point stitched to the centre it was given to and drawn with that centre's mark. Press the button and the centres move; press again and some points switch sides. After a few rounds no point switches and the centres stop moving. The algorithm has **converged**, and each point belongs to the cluster whose centre is closest.

The assignment rule is plain Euclidean distance:

$$\text{cluster}(\mathbf{x}_i) = \arg\min_j \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2$$

It is the same distance formula as KNN. The difference is what you measure to: KNN looks at the nearest **data points**, k-means looks at the nearest **cluster centres**. The rule also carves the whole plane into territories, one per centre, each holding every location that is closer to that centre than to any other (a Voronoi diagram).

The update rule is where the name comes from. The centre of cluster $j$ is the **mean** of the points assigned to it:

$$\boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j} \mathbf{x}_i$$

## The total it lowers

Both half-steps serve one number, the **total within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS)**:

$$\min \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2$$

| Symbol | What it is | Plain English |
|:------:|:-----------|:-------------|
| $k$ | Number of clusters | How many groups you want |
| $C_j$ | Cluster $j$ | The set of points assigned to group $j$ |
| $\mathbf{x}_i$ | A data point | One observation |
| $\boldsymbol{\mu}_j$ | Center (centroid) of cluster $j$ | The average of all points in group $j$ |
| $\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2$ | Squared distance | How far point $i$ is from its cluster center |

In plain words: make each point as close as possible to the centre of its assigned cluster. Tight clusters mean a low WCSS, and a low WCSS is good. In Fig. 2 it is the readout at the top right, the squared lengths of all the threads added up, and you can watch it fall with every press.

## A different start, a different answer

The loop is a heuristic. It always stops, but where it stops depends on where it began. k-means starts from **random** centres, and different starting positions can lead to different results, sometimes bad ones.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="kmeans-figure" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 3 · the same points and the same k, from another start · made-up data"}
:::

This run has converged. No point wants to switch and no centre wants to move, yet the total is far above the best one found. The algorithm cannot see that; it only ever compares a point with the centres it currently has. Press "new start" to try other seeded starts, or drag a centre somewhere and press "run".

The fix is to run k-means many times from different random starts and keep the result with the **lowest WCSS**. In R, `kmeans(data, centers = k, nstart = 20)` does the 20 runs for you. More starts make the best clustering more likely to turn up, with diminishing returns past about 20. [A single run is not guaranteed to find the best clustering. It can get stuck in a bad solution. Use `nstart`.]{.side}

## How many groups?

The hardest part of k-means is that you must choose $k$ in advance. The algorithm cannot decide for you, and there is no formula. What you have is the **elbow method**: run k-means for $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, record the total WCSS for each, plot $k$ against WCSS, and look for the elbow, the place where the curve bends and adding more clusters stops helping much.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="kmeans-figure" data-step="3" data-caption="Fig. 4 · the best of 20 starts for each k, computed in your browser · made-up data"}
:::

Here going from 2 clusters to 3 gives a big drop in WCSS and going from 3 to 4 gives almost nothing, so the elbow bends at 3. The elbow is a **judgment call**, not an exact calculation. Sometimes it is obvious and sometimes it is ambiguous. [The two k's are different things. In KNN, k is the number of neighbours. In k-means, k is the number of clusters.]{.side}

## What to watch for

Know the difference between supervised and unsupervised cold.

| | Supervised (SVM, KNN) | Unsupervised (k-means) |
|:--|:----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Labels?** | Yes — you know the groups | No — groups are unknown |
| **Goal** | Learn the rule to predict labels | Discover hidden structure |
| **Evaluation** | Accuracy, cross-validation | WCSS, silhouette, elbow method |
| **k means...** | (KNN) number of neighbors | (k-means) number of clusters |
| **Example** | "Is this email spam?" | "What types of customers do we have?" |

Scaling is mandatory, for the same reason as in KNN and SVM. k-means uses distance, so an unscaled feature with a large range dominates. Cluster customers on income in dollars and age in years and income alone decides the groups. [Scale first. Every distance-based method on this site needs it: KNN, SVM and k-means.]{.side}

k-means also assumes spherical clusters. Its boundaries are equidistant from the centres, which produces round, convex regions, so data with elongated, curved or irregular shapes will not cluster well. Two concentric rings are the standard failure: it cannot wrap one cluster around another. It is sensitive to outliers too, because a single extreme point can pull a centre away.

The classic use is customer segmentation. You have customer data, no labels, and the business wants to know what types of customers it has. The workflow: collect the customer features (spend, visits, demographics), scale them, use the elbow method to choose $k$, run k-means with `nstart = 20`, interpret the clusters and give them business-meaningful names, then build a different strategy for each segment.

## Run it yourself {.reference}

Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Three hidden clusters, shown the way you would actually meet them: without the labels.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unlabeled
#| fig-cap: "You see the data. Can you spot the groups? k-means can."

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

# Three hidden clusters
true_centers <- data.frame(x1 = c(2, 6, 4), x2 = c(2, 2, 6))
n_per <- 60

df <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(n_per, 2, 0.7), rnorm(n_per, 6, 0.7), rnorm(n_per, 4, 0.7)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(n_per, 2, 0.7), rnorm(n_per, 2, 0.7), rnorm(n_per, 6, 0.7)),
  true_group = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = n_per))
)

# Show without labels
ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2",
       title = "All you see: unlabeled points")
```

Six rounds of the algorithm written out by hand: assign every point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points.

```{r}
#| label: plot-algorithm-steps
#| fig-cap: "k-means in action: assign → move centers → assign → move → converge"

set.seed(15)

# Manual k-means to show each step
k <- 3
centers <- df[sample(nrow(df), k), c("x1", "x2")]
colors <- c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 3, 1))

for (iter in 1:6) {
  # Step 2: Assign to nearest center
  dists <- sapply(1:k, function(j) {
    sqrt((df$x1 - centers$x1[j])^2 + (df$x2 - centers$x2[j])^2)
  })
  assignments <- apply(dists, 1, which.min)

  plot(df$x1, df$x2,
    col = adjustcolor(colors[assignments], 0.5),
    pch = 19, cex = 1,
    main = paste("Iteration", iter),
    xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2")

  # Show centers
  points(centers$x1, centers$x2, pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 3,
         col = colors[1:k])

  # Draw lines from centers to their points (first iteration only)
  if (iter == 1) {
    legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.7,
      legend = "✕ = cluster centers")
  }

  # Step 3: Move centers
  for (j in 1:k) {
    members <- df[assignments == j, ]
    centers$x1[j] <- mean(members$x1)
    centers$x2[j] <- mean(members$x2)
  }
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The fitted result from `kmeans()`, with a line from every point to its centre. The squared lengths of those lines add up to the WCSS in the title.

```{r}
#| label: plot-wcss-visual
#| fig-cap: "WCSS = sum of all these distances (squared). k-means tries to make this small."

# Final k-means result
km <- kmeans(df[, c("x1", "x2")], centers = 3, nstart = 20)

df$cluster <- factor(km$cluster)
centers_final <- as.data.frame(km$centers)
centers_final$cluster <- factor(1:3)

ggplot(df, aes(x1, x2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = km$centers[as.numeric(cluster), 1],
                    yend = km$centers[as.numeric(cluster), 2]),
               alpha = 0.15, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = centers_final, aes(x1, x2),
             shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 3, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2",
       title = paste("Total WCSS =", round(km$tot.withinss, 1)),
       subtitle = "Each line = distance from point to its center") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The territories. Every location on the plane belongs to its nearest centre.

```{r}
#| label: plot-voronoi
#| fig-cap: "Each region contains all points closest to that center (Voronoi diagram)"

# Show decision regions
grid <- expand.grid(
  x1 = seq(min(df$x1) - 1, max(df$x1) + 1, length.out = 200),
  x2 = seq(min(df$x2) - 1, max(df$x2) + 1, length.out = 200)
)

dists_grid <- sapply(1:3, function(j) {
  sqrt((grid$x1 - km$centers[j, 1])^2 + (grid$x2 - km$centers[j, 2])^2)
})
grid$cluster <- factor(apply(dists_grid, 1, which.min))

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = grid, aes(x1, x2, fill = cluster), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x1, x2, color = cluster), size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = centers_final, aes(x1, x2),
             shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 3, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2",
       title = "Cluster territories: every location maps to its nearest center") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The elbow method: fit $k = 1$ to $10$, record the total WCSS for each, and look for the bend.

```{r}
#| label: plot-elbow
#| fig-cap: "The elbow method: WCSS drops sharply, then flattens — the bend is your k"

k_range <- 1:10
wcss <- sapply(k_range, function(k) {
  km_fit <- kmeans(df[, c("x1", "x2")], centers = k, nstart = 20)
  km_fit$tot.withinss
})

elbow_df <- data.frame(k = k_range, wcss = wcss)

ggplot(elbow_df, aes(k, wcss)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = elbow_df[3, ], aes(k, wcss),
             size = 6, shape = 1, color = "coral", stroke = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = wcss[3],
           label = "Elbow at k = 3", color = "coral", size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.2, xend = 3.2, y = wcss[3], yend = wcss[3],
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), color = "coral") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_range) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Number of Clusters (k)", y = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares",
       title = "Elbow Method: Where does adding clusters stop helping?")
```

The same data and the same $k = 3$ from three different random starts, one start each.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bad-init
#| fig-cap: "Same data, same k=3, but different random starts → different results"

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 3, 1))

colors <- c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")

for (trial in c(1, 2, 3)) {
  set.seed(trial * 7)
  km_trial <- kmeans(df[, c("x1", "x2")], centers = 3, nstart = 1)

  plot(df$x1, df$x2,
    col = adjustcolor(colors[km_trial$cluster], 0.6),
    pch = 19, cex = 1,
    main = paste0("Start #", trial, " (WCSS = ", round(km_trial$tot.withinss, 0), ")"),
    xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2")
  points(km_trial$centers[, 1], km_trial$centers[, 2],
         pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 3)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The average WCSS found as `nstart` grows. More starts find the better answer more reliably.

```{r}
#| label: plot-nstart
#| fig-cap: "More random starts → more likely to find the best clustering"

nstart_vals <- c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50)
best_wcss <- sapply(nstart_vals, function(ns) {
  results <- replicate(20, {
    km_fit <- kmeans(df[, c("x1", "x2")], centers = 3, nstart = ns)
    km_fit$tot.withinss
  })
  mean(results)
})

ggplot(data.frame(nstart = nstart_vals, wcss = best_wcss), aes(nstart, wcss)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "nstart (number of random starts)", y = "Average WCSS found",
       title = "More starts = better solution (diminishing returns past ~20)")
```

Income and age, clustered raw and then scaled. Without scaling, income decides everything.

```{r}
#| label: plot-scaling-kmeans
#| fig-cap: "Without scaling, the high-range feature dominates cluster assignments"

set.seed(42)

# Customer data: income (30k-90k) and age (18-70)
customers <- data.frame(
  income = c(rnorm(40, 40000, 5000), rnorm(40, 75000, 5000)),
  age = c(rnorm(40, 25, 4), rnorm(40, 55, 4))
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Unscaled
km_raw <- kmeans(customers, 2, nstart = 20)
plot(customers$income, customers$age,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue")[km_raw$cluster],
  pch = 19, main = "Unscaled: income dominates",
  xlab = "Income ($)", ylab = "Age")

# Scaled
cust_scaled <- scale(customers)
km_scaled <- kmeans(cust_scaled, 2, nstart = 20)
plot(customers$income, customers$age,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue")[km_scaled$cluster],
  pch = 19, main = "Scaled: both features contribute",
  xlab = "Income ($)", ylab = "Age")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The same points with labels given (supervised) and with clusters discovered (unsupervised).

```{r}
#| label: plot-supervised-vs-unsupervised
#| fig-cap: "Left: supervised (labels known, learn boundary). Right: unsupervised (no labels, find groups)."

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Supervised: labeled data with boundary
plot(df$x1, df$x2,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")[as.numeric(df$true_group)],
  pch = 19, cex = 1.2,
  main = "Supervised: labels given",
  xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")
legend("topleft", legend = c("A", "B", "C"), bty = "n",
  col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"), pch = 19, cex = 0.8,
  title = "Known labels")

# Unsupervised: same data, no labels, discover clusters
plot(df$x1, df$x2,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen")[km$cluster],
  pch = 19, cex = 1.2,
  main = "Unsupervised: clusters discovered",
  xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2")
points(km$centers[, 1], km$centers[, 2], pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 3)
legend("topleft", legend = paste("Cluster", 1:3), bty = "n",
  col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"), pch = 19, cex = 0.8,
  title = "Discovered groups")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Two concentric rings, which k-means cannot separate.

```{r}
#| label: plot-limitations
#| fig-cap: "k-means struggles with non-spherical shapes"

set.seed(42)

# Concentric rings (k-means will fail)
n <- 200
angle <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
r_inner <- rnorm(n / 2, 1.5, 0.2)
r_outer <- rnorm(n / 2, 4, 0.3)

rings <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(r_inner * cos(angle[1:(n/2)]), r_outer * cos(angle[(n/2+1):n])),
  x2 = c(r_inner * sin(angle[1:(n/2)]), r_outer * sin(angle[(n/2+1):n])),
  true = factor(rep(c("Inner", "Outer"), each = n / 2))
)

km_rings <- kmeans(rings[, 1:2], 2, nstart = 20)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

plot(rings$x1, rings$x2,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue")[as.numeric(rings$true)],
  pch = 19, main = "True groups (rings)",
  xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", asp = 1)

plot(rings$x1, rings$x2,
  col = c("coral", "steelblue")[km_rings$cluster],
  pch = 19, main = "k-means result (wrong!)",
  xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", asp = 1)
points(km_rings$centers[, 1], km_rings$centers[, 2],
       pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Customer segmentation from start to finish: scale, cluster, then name the segments.

```{r}
#| label: plot-segmentation
#| fig-cap: "Customer segmentation: k-means discovers 3 natural groups from spending data"

set.seed(42)

# Simulated customer data
customers2 <- data.frame(
  annual_spend = c(rnorm(50, 200, 40), rnorm(50, 600, 80), rnorm(50, 1200, 150)),
  visit_frequency = c(rnorm(50, 4, 1), rnorm(50, 12, 2), rnorm(50, 25, 3))
)

# Scale then cluster
cust_s <- scale(customers2)
km_cust <- kmeans(cust_s, 3, nstart = 20)

customers2$segment <- factor(km_cust$cluster)

# Label segments meaningfully
seg_means <- aggregate(cbind(annual_spend, visit_frequency) ~ segment, data = customers2, mean)
seg_means <- seg_means[order(seg_means$annual_spend), ]
seg_labels <- c("Budget Shoppers", "Regular Customers", "VIP / High-Value")

ggplot(customers2, aes(annual_spend, visit_frequency, color = segment)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"),
                     labels = seg_labels) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Annual Spend ($)", y = "Visit Frequency (per month)",
       color = "Segment",
       title = "k-means segmentation: 3 customer groups discovered")
```

## On one page {.reference}

```
THE k-MEANS RECIPE
===================

1. ALGORITHM (repeat until convergence):
   - Assign each point to nearest center
   - Move each center to mean of its points

2. THE FORMULA:

   min  Σⱼ Σᵢ∈Cⱼ ||xᵢ - μⱼ||²
        -------------------------
        "total distance from points
         to their cluster centers"

   Center of cluster j:  μⱼ = (1/|Cⱼ|) × Σ xᵢ

3. KEY PARAMETER:
   k → number of clusters (choose via elbow method)

4. ELBOW METHOD:
   Plot k vs WCSS → pick the "bend" point

5. GOTCHAS:
   - Random initialization → use nstart = 20
   - ALWAYS scale features first
   - Assumes spherical clusters
   - You must choose k in advance

6. SUPERVISED vs UNSUPERVISED:
   Labels → supervised (SVM, KNN)
   No labels → unsupervised (k-means)

7. PRACTICE TIP:
   "Segment customers" / "find groups" / "no labels" → k-means
   "Classify" / "predict category" / "labeled data" → SVM, KNN
```
